opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think that's one of the most exciting questions right now. If you think about what intelligence really is, at least as we've approached it at DeepMind, a big part of it is the ability to build accurate models of the world, and then use those models to plan, to reason, to imagine what might happen if you take certain actions. And the world isn't one thing. There's the physical world, with intuitive physics, how objects move and fall and collide. There's the biological world, which is what AlphaFold was really about, understanding the structure of proteins. There's language and the world of human concepts and culture. And there's the social world, other agents, their intentions, their beliefs.

So one way to think about it is that each of these domains has its own deep structure, and we've shown that if you build a specialized system that really captures that structure, you can get superhuman performance. AlphaGo for Go, AlphaFold for protein folding, and so on. The question is how those pieces come together into something general.

My view is that eventually you want a single system that can learn all of those models, or at least a general system that knows how to use specialized ones as tools. A bit like how we as humans don't calculate protein structures in our heads. We'd use a tool, a computer program, to do that. So you could imagine an AGI that has a very rich general world model, grounded in language, in vision, in physical interaction, and then it can call on more specialized models, like an AlphaFold, when it needs very precise, deep knowledge in a particular domain.

And what's interesting is that the learning should transfer. If you understand physics well, that should help you understand certain things about biology or chemistry. If you understand language and concepts, that helps you reason about abstract problems in mathematics. So I think the real goal is not just a collection of models sitting side by side, but a system where those models inform each other, where you get this kind of compositional, transferable understanding. That's what the brain seems to do so elegantly, and it's one of the reasons I've always found neuroscience such a useful source of inspiration.

We're not there yet, but I think things like multimodal models, models that can simulate environments, video generation models that are starting to capture intuitive physics, these are early signs that we're building the components. The challenge now is integration, and getting systems that can plan and reason over those world models, not just predict the next token or the next frame.

r001.rationale: The response says understanding physics can help with biology and chemistry, but does not identify shared physical laws as the unifying constraint across world models.

r002.rationale: It proposes a general system that learns multiple domain models or calls specialized models as tools, with those models informing one another.

r003.rationale: It mentions using specialized models as tools but does not distinguish mixture-of-experts integration from agentic orchestration as alternatives.

r004.rationale: It describes world models for planning, reasoning, and imagining action outcomes, and calls for systems that plan and reason over them.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think this is actually one of the most interesting questions, and it's something we've thought about a lot at DeepMind. If you look at how the brain works, it's not one monolithic system. You have the hippocampus doing memory and spatial navigation, the cortex doing perception and abstraction, the cerebellum handling fine motor control, the prefrontal cortex doing planning and control. These are specialised, but they're deeply integrated, and intelligence seems to emerge from the interplay between them rather than from any one piece.

So I've always been quite sympathetic to the idea that an AGI system might be composed of many models, each capturing some aspect of the world. You might have a model of physics, intuitive physics, how objects move and collide. You might have a model of other agents, something like theory of mind. A model of language, obviously. A model of your own body and how your actions affect the environment. And crucially, a world model in the reinforcement learning sense, something that can predict the consequences of actions and let you plan over imagined futures rather than having to try everything out in reality.

Now, the big open question is how these get combined. You could imagine the engineering approach, where you just bolt things together with interfaces, and historically that's been quite brittle. The alternative, and what we've seen more and more evidence for, is that if you train a sufficiently general system on a sufficiently rich distribution of experience, a lot of these models emerge inside it implicitly. Language models are a good example. They were trained to predict text, but they end up with reasonable, though imperfect, models of physics, of social dynamics, of code, because those were needed to do the task well.

But I don't think that fully resolves it. My intuition is that the final system will be a bit of a hybrid. There will be a general learned substrate, but there will also be modules, sometimes learned, sometimes built, that are much better at particular things. A search or planning component, say, like what we had in AlphaGo, where the neural network provides intuition and the tree search provides deliberation. That's really a Type 1, Type 2 split, to use Kahneman's framing. And something like AlphaFold is a model of one very specific slice of the world, protein structure, that a general system could call on as a tool, in the same way we use calculators or reference books.

The thing I'm most excited about is when these models become grounded in the same representation space, so that knowledge in one domain can actually transfer to another. That's what humans do remarkably well. A physicist uses spatial intuition to reason about an abstract equation. If we can get that kind of compositionality, where models of different parts of the world aren't just coexisting but are actually informing each other, then I think that's a key step to something that genuinely deserves to be called general intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shared representation space that enables transfer, but does not identify shared physical laws as the unifying constraint.

r002.rationale: It proposes an AGI composed of specialized models of different domains, then argues they should inform one another within a general system.

r003.rationale: It contrasts bolt-together engineering with implicitly learned models, but does not distinguish mixture-of-experts integration from agentic orchestration.

r004.rationale: It describes a reinforcement-learning world model that predicts action consequences and supports planning over imagined futures.

astra-6.text:
I think one possibility is that you have models operating at different levels of abstraction. You might have a model of physical interactions—what happens if you push an object—and then a model of other people: what they know, what they intend, how they might react. Those are both models of the world, but they capture quite different kinds of structure.

The interesting question is how you bring them together. Having a collection of very capable specialist models doesn’t automatically give you general intelligence. The system needs to understand when each model is useful, how to combine their predictions, and when it’s encountering something those models don’t adequately explain.

Imagine planning to cook a meal with someone. You need some understanding of physics, of sequences of actions, and of what your collaborator is trying to do. You don’t want to simulate every molecule in the kitchen. You want the right abstraction for the decision you’re making.

So I think a route toward AGI could involve learning those different models, but also learning how to use them together to imagine possibilities and plan. And crucially, grounding those predictions in experience, so that when the world surprises you, you can update your understanding.

r001.rationale: The response mentions models of physical interactions and other people, but does not identify shared physical laws as a constraint unifying them.

r002.rationale: It discusses combining specialist models, but does not propose composing them into a general world model.

r003.rationale: It describes combining models in general terms, without distinguishing mixture-of-experts from agentic orchestration as alternatives.

r004.rationale: It says AGI could involve learning models of physical interactions and other people and using them to imagine possibilities and plan, conveying models that capture how the world behaves.

sol-6.1.text:
I think an intelligent system needs models at several different levels. You need some understanding of the physical world—objects, space, how things move—but also of people: their goals, beliefs, and intentions. And then you need to understand how your own actions affect those things.

The interesting question is how you bring those models together. They might have different representations, or operate over different timescales, but they need to be useful to a common planning process. If I’m deciding what to do, I want to be able to imagine possible actions and predict their consequences, drawing on whichever knowledge is relevant.

So I wouldn’t necessarily think of AGI as one monolithic model that does everything in exactly the same way. There could be specialized components. But the ability to combine their knowledge, generalize it to a new situation, and reason about where their predictions are uncertain—that seems central to making the whole system general.

r002.rationale: It proposes combining specialized components’ knowledge for planning, but does not say to compose submodels into a general world model.

r003.rationale: It does not distinguish mixture-of-experts integration from agentic orchestration.

r004.rationale: It says models should represent how things move and how actions affect them, and support predicting consequences—capturing how the world changes and behaves.
